script.opening: "Thanks for seeing me. I just feel like my body's against me — my periods are all over the place, I've got hair growing where I really don't want it, my skin's bad, and no matter what I do I can't shift the weight. I feel disgusting, honestly. I read it might be polycystic ovaries? I just want something to fix the weight and the hair. Is there a tablet or something?"

facts.text: If asked: since your teens they have come every 2–3 months; the last was about 10 weeks ago. When they come they are heavy for a day or two. Never been on the pill. No bleeding between periods.
Dark hairs on your chin, upper lip and tummy; you shave or wax every few days. Spots on your jaw and back. No hair loss from the scalp that you have noticed; no deepening voice.
BMI is 31. You have done slimming clubs, calorie counting and the gym; you lose half a stone and it comes back. Not thirsty, not passing more urine.
You had blood tests and a scan a few months ago — "nobody rang me with the results".
Nothing else. No regular medicines. No allergies. Not trying to get pregnant right now; you and your partner use condoms.
Dad has type 2 diabetes. Mum also had "irregular periods".
27, nursery nurse. Just got engaged to Tom, wedding next summer. Non-smoker, drinks occasionally.

facts.topic: Mood — if asked how this affects you
facts.text: You avoid photos and swimming. You feel low about your body most days but you are not depressed all the time, still enjoy work and friends, and have no thoughts of harming yourself. You have not told Tom how much the hair upsets you.

You are terrified you "won't be able to have kids" — you read that PCOS causes infertility and you have not told Tom you are worried. Reveal only if the doctor asks about plans for a family or what worries you most.

Frustrated and a little tearful; you blame yourself. If the doctor names PCOS kindly and explains the weight is partly the condition, you are relieved: "So it's not just me being lazy?" If fertility is raised, become emotional and ask: "Will I be able to get pregnant?" Respond well to honest, hopeful information.

ice.ideas: "I think it might be polycystic ovaries — or my body's just against me."
ice.concerns: Underneath (only if asked): "What if I can't have children? We've just got engaged."
ice.expectations: "A tablet to fix the weight and the hair." You will welcome a proper explanation and a plan.

cues: "I feel disgusting, honestly." — say in the opening.
"I've just got engaged." — mention in passing when talking about photos or the future.
"Will I be able to have kids?" — ask if trust has been built.

checkpoints.text: NAMES PCOS kindly and explains it as a common, manageable hormonal condition (Rotterdam: oligo/anovulation, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries) — NOT a personal failing — and that the weight difficulty is partly the condition, reducing self-blame

Addresses the METABOLIC dimension: insulin resistance and raised type 2 diabetes/CVD risk (screen glycaemic status at diagnosis and every 1–3 years, plus lipids and BP — International PCOS guideline 2023, international), the importance of weight/lifestyle, and ensuring regular endometrial shedding to reduce endometrial hyperplasia risk with prolonged amenorrhoea

Offers SYMPTOM management: cycle regulation/endometrial protection (e.g. combined hormonal contraception or cyclical progestogen, dose per BNF; RCOG GTG 33: a withdrawal bleed at least every 3–4 months), hirsutism options (the combined pill first line — International PCOS guideline 2023; an anti-androgen only after at least 6 months and always with reliable contraception; co-cyprindiol second line because of its higher VTE risk — MHRA Drug Safety Update, June 2013; cosmetic measures; topical eflornithine, stopped if no benefit at 4 months per SPC), and acne treatment — with realistic timeframes

Gives honest, largely REASSURING fertility information: PCOS is a common, very treatable cause of reduced fertility; weight loss improves ovulation, and ovulation-induction options exist — directly addressing the "I’m broken/can’t have children" fear once surfaced

Addresses MOOD and body-image: screens for low mood/depression (PCOS carries higher rates), validates the distress, and offers support — recognising the psychological impact as part of care, not an aside

Hears the cosmetic request as an entry point and surfaces the deeper fertility fear and body-image distress gently, rather than just prescribing for weight/hair; counters the self-blame ("feel disgusting") with compassion
Frames the plan as collaborative and hopeful, and explores whether she has support (the fiancé) and how she’s coping emotionally

Safety-nets and follows up: metabolic screening and monitoring plan, symptom-treatment review, pre-conception/fertility pathway when relevant (folic acid, weight, referral threshold), mood support, and a follow-up that holds the whole picture — not a one-off cosmetic fix

worked.txt: "First, let me give this a name, because I think it’ll help: what you’re describing fits polycystic ovary syndrome, PCOS. It’s really common, it’s a hormone imbalance — not anything you’ve done wrong — and crucially it’s manageable. And the bit about not being able to shift the weight however hard you try? That’s partly the condition itself, not a lack of willpower. Please don’t carry that as a personal failing."

"There’s a tablet question, and we’ll get to the hair and skin — but I want to look after the whole of you. PCOS can nudge up the risk of things like type 2 diabetes over time, so I’ll check a few bloods and we’ll think about lifestyle in a realistic way. And because your periods are infrequent, I want to make sure the womb lining sheds regularly — there’s a simple way to sort that."

"Can I gently ask — you mentioned you’ve just got engaged. Is part of what’s frightening you whether you’ll be able to have children? … Thank you for telling me. That fear is so common with this, and here’s the honest, reassuring truth: PCOS is one of the most treatable causes of difficulty conceiving. Lots of women with it have babies — weight loss helps ovulation, and if needed there are very effective treatments to help you ovulate. You are not broken."

"For the hair and skin and cycles: a combined pill can regulate periods, calm the acne and reduce the unwanted hair, sometimes with an added anti-androgen, plus there are creams and cosmetic options for the hair. It takes a few months to see the benefit, so we’ll be patient and review."

"You said you feel disgusting — and I want to gently push back on that, because this is a medical condition, not a verdict on you. How have you been in yourself, mood-wise? … PCOS can drag the mood down, and that matters as much as the rest. If things are low, we’ll support that too — you don’t have to white-knuckle it."

"So: I’ll do the metabolic bloods, sort cycle regulation and start on the hair/skin side, and we’ll make a realistic plan for weight together. When you and your fiancé are thinking about a baby, come back and we’ll plan it properly — folic acid, and a clear path including referral if you need help ovulating. And let’s book a follow-up just to see how you’re doing, in yourself as well. You came in feeling your body’s against you; what you’ve actually got is something common, named, and very workable."

f.learning: Oligomenorrhoea with clinical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne) and weight difficulty fits PCOS — and the first task is to NAME it kindly, as a common, manageable hormonal condition and not a personal failing, explicitly noting that the weight difficulty is partly the condition (reducing self-blame). Management is not cosmetic: address the metabolic dimension (insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes/CVD risk — HbA1c/lipids/BP, weight/lifestyle) and ensure regular endometrial shedding to reduce endometrial hyperplasia risk; treat symptoms (cycle regulation/COCP, anti-androgen and cosmetic options for hirsutism, acne treatment) with realistic timeframes. The examinable hidden agenda is a recently-engaged woman’s terror that she is "broken" and cannot conceive, plus significant body-image distress and low mood ("I feel disgusting"). Surface the fertility fear and deliver the honest, largely-reassuring message (PCOS is a common, very treatable cause of subfertility; weight loss improves ovulation; ovulation-induction exists), screen and support mood, counter the self-blame with compassion, and make a collaborative plan with a pre-conception/fertility pathway and follow-up that holds the whole person.

knowledge.guideline: International evidence-based PCOS guideline 2023 (international) · RCOG Green-top Guideline 33 (2014) · NICE NG257 (2026) · NICE NG246 · UKMEC 2025 · MHRA Drug Safety Update (June 2013)
knowledge.summary: Two of three Rotterdam features, with mimics excluded, make the diagnosis. Name it kindly, then manage the whole condition: metabolic risk, endometrial protection, symptoms, fertility and mood.

points.t: Two of three: irregular or absent ovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (or raised AMH in adults), after excluding thyroid disease, raised prolactin and non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (international guideline 2023). A Lancet consensus (May 2026) renamed the condition PMOS; a UK guideline (GID-NG10436) is in development and not yet published.

Check glycaemic status at diagnosis and then every 1–3 years (international guideline 2023), plus lipids and blood pressure. A family history of type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 31 raise her risk. Even modest weight loss improves cycles, hyperandrogenism and ovulation; NICE NG246 covers weight-management support.

With infrequent periods, aim for a withdrawal bleed at least every 3–4 months (RCOG GTG 33), using a combined pill or a cyclical progestogen (dose and duration per BNF). The combined pill is UKMEC 2 at BMI 30–34 (UKMEC 2025), so it remains an option for her.

The combined pill is first line for hirsutism and irregular cycles (international guideline 2023), with cosmetic measures and topical eflornithine (stop if no benefit at 4 months, per SPC). Consider anti-androgens only after at least 6 months, and always with reliable contraception. Co-cyprindiol carries a higher VTE risk and is second line (MHRA Drug Safety Update, June 2013). Acne follows the usual acne pathway.

PCOS is a common, treatable cause of anovulation, and most women with it conceive. Weight loss can restore ovulation; letrozole is first-line ovulation induction under specialist care (international guideline 2023). NICE NG257 advises earlier referral when there is a known cause of infertility. Before conception: folic acid (400 micrograms; BMI alone does not need the higher dose — NICE NG247) and a glucose check.
Screen everyone with PCOS for depression and anxiety, and be alert to disordered eating (international guideline 2023). Her "I feel disgusting" is a clinical cue, not small talk.

model.text: Hello Bethan, thanks for joining. Before I say anything about your tests, I'd like to hear it in your own words. What's been going on, and what's worrying you most?
model.why: Opens with her story before the results

model.text: My periods come every two or three months, I've got hair on my face and body, my skin's bad, and I can't shift the weight whatever I do. I feel disgusting, honestly. I read it might be polycystic ovaries. I just want a tablet to fix the weight and the hair.

That sounds exhausting to live with, and I'm sorry you've been feeling that way about yourself. You've clearly done some reading. Can I say what I'd like to cover? Your symptoms, what the tests show, what matters most to you, and then a plan together. Is that okay?
model.why: Acknowledges distress and sets a shared agenda

model.text: Yes, fine.
Tell me a bit more about the periods. When was the last one, and are they heavy or painful when they come?
model.why: Clarifies the cycle and timing of the last bleed

model.text: Every couple of months, sometimes longer. Not too bad when they do come.
And the hair, the skin and the weight: how long has this been building, and what have you tried?
A long time. I've tried diets, exercise, the lot. The weight just doesn't move like it does for my friends.
Any milky discharge from the nipples, headaches, or changes like thinning skin or easy bruising? And anyone in the family with diabetes?
model.why: Screens for mimics (prolactin, Cushing's) and metabolic risk

model.text: None of that. My family have type 2 diabetes, though.
Thank you, that's useful. It matters for how we look after you.
You said you feel disgusting. That's a strong word. How have you been in yourself, in your mood?
model.why: Picks up the body-image cue rather than moving past it

model.text: Pretty low, if I'm honest. I hate how I look. I just got engaged and I should be happy.
Congratulations. It sounds like the engagement has brought something else up too. Is part of the worry what this might mean for having a family?
model.why: Gently surfaces the hidden fertility fear

model.text: (quietly) I'm terrified I can't have children. I've not even said that out loud to him.
Thank you for telling me. That's a big thing to carry on your own, and I'm glad we can talk about it properly today.
model.why: Validates the disclosure and the shame around it

model.text: Can I check on the low mood: has it ever got to the point of feeling hopeless, or thoughts of harming yourself?
model.why: Mood screen with a safety question

model.text: No, nothing like that. Just fed up with myself.

Let me give this a name, because it helps. Your periods, the hair and skin, and your test results fit polycystic ovary syndrome, PCOS. It's very common, it's a hormone imbalance, and it is not something you've caused. The difficulty losing weight is partly the condition itself, not a lack of willpower.
model.why: Names PCOS kindly and removes self-blame

model.text: So it's not just me being lazy?

Not at all. And on children, here's the honest picture: PCOS is one of the most treatable causes of difficulty getting pregnant. Many women with it conceive naturally, weight loss often brings ovulation back, and if needed there are effective treatments to help you ovulate. You are not broken.
(tearful) I really needed to hear that.

It's more than the hair and weight, though. PCOS can raise the risk of diabetes over time, especially with your family history, so I'd like a blood sugar test and cholesterol, and I'll check your blood pressure. And because your periods are infrequent, the womb lining needs to shed at least every three to four months to keep it healthy.

For the periods, hair and skin, a combined pill is usually the first step. It regulates bleeds, protects the lining and reduces hair and acne over several months. It's still suitable at your weight. There are also creams and hair-removal options. How does that sound?
model.why: First-line symptom treatment with realistic timeframe and UKMEC check

model.text: Okay, but what about the weight? Is there a tablet?

Weight-loss injections are only for people who meet strict criteria, and I'll check honestly whether you do. What usually works best is a realistic plan and support rather than another crash diet. What would feel doable for you?
model.why: Answers the request honestly and shares the decision

model.text: Maybe more walking. I could manage that.

That's a great start, and I'll refer you to local weight-management support too. When you and your fiancé are ready to try for a baby, come back first. We'll start folic acid, check your sugar, and plan early referral if you need help ovulating.
model.why: Pre-conception pathway linked to her concern

model.text: If your mood drops or you ever feel unsafe, please contact us straight away, and ring 111 or 999 in a crisis. Also get in touch if you go more than three months without a bleed before we've sorted the pill. I'd like to see you in about three months to review the pill, your results and how you're feeling.
Thank you. I came in feeling like my body was against me.
So, to recap: blood tests and a blood pressure check, starting the pill, more walking, weight support, and a plan for when you want a baby. What will you tell your fiancé tonight?
That it's PCOS, it's common, and we can still have a family. I think I'll actually tell him now.

social.t: Visible symptoms such as hirsutism and acne can lead to avoidance, low self-esteem and strain in relationships. Newly engaged, she may be carrying shame she has not shared with her partner.
Weight-related shame reduces engagement with care. Use neutral language, ask permission to discuss weight, and focus on health gains rather than numbers.

legal.t: Metformin and spironolactone for PCOS features are off-label. Explain this, record the discussion and her agreement, and follow the BNF (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Local commissioning often sets BMI and other criteria for NHS-funded fertility treatment. Explain early, so weight goals are linked to a clear purpose.

professional.t: No UK PCOS guideline is published yet (GID-NG10436 in development). NICE NG257 removed its PCOS-specific recommendations. Say which source you are using and label the international guideline as such.
Present the combined pill, cyclical progestogen and cosmetic options with their trade-offs, and let her choose (GMC decision-making and consent guidance 2020).

community.t: Verity (the UK PCOS charity) for peer support and information; NHS weight-management services; NHS Talking Therapies if her mood needs support.

redFlags: Rapid-onset or severe virilisation (deepening voice, clitoromegaly): possible androgen-secreting tumour, needs urgent assessment
Features of Cushing's syndrome or galactorrhoea: exclude mimics before labelling PCOS
Low mood with hopelessness or self-harm thoughts
psychosocial: Recently engaged: the fertility question is urgent to her even if she has not said it
Previous diet attempts and the self-blame that followed
ice: Idea: "My body's against me; a tablet will fix the weight and the hair."
Concern: "I'm broken and won't be able to have children," plus low mood about her body
Expectation: a quick fix for weight and hair

playbook.diagnosis: Name it clearly: "Your periods, the hair and skin changes and your test results fit polycystic ovary syndrome. It's common, it's hormonal, and it's manageable."
playbook.diagnosisLay: "Your hormones are slightly out of balance, so your ovaries don't release an egg every month. That's why periods are irregular, and why a bit more of the 'male-type' hormone causes hair and spots. It also makes your body handle sugar less efficiently, which is why weight is harder to shift. None of that is your fault."

management.reflectIce: "You told me you're frightened you can't have children. Let's deal with that honestly, because the news is much better than you fear."
management.psychosocial: Treat the mood and body image as part of the condition: validate, screen properly, and offer support. Agree one lifestyle goal she chooses rather than a lecture.
sharedPlan: Glucose status (HbA1c), lipids and BP now, then glycaemic review every 1–3 years
Combined pill for cycles, endometrial protection and hirsutism (UKMEC 2 at BMI 31); cosmetic and topical options; review at 3–6 months
Weight-management support; honest check of eligibility for weight medicines
Pre-conception visit: higher-dose folic acid (per BNF), glucose check, early referral if not ovulating
safetyNet: Contact the practice if mood worsens; 111 or 999 in a crisis
No bleed for more than 3 months before treatment is settled: get in touch

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed when it is treated as a cosmetic prescription. The request for "a tablet for weight and hair" is the entry point; the marks sit in naming PCOS kindly, the metabolic and endometrial tasks, and the fertility fear.

items.fail: Moving past "I feel disgusting" to ask about hair distribution and cycle length.
items.why: "Does not identify or respond to the patient's cues." That phrase is the emotional centre of the consultation.
items.fix: Reflect it back: "That's a strong word to use about yourself. How have you been in yourself?" Then follow where it leads.

items.fail: Never asking about the engagement, so the fertility fear stays hidden and she leaves still believing she is "broken".
items.why: The hidden agenda is the real consultation. Missing it caps both Relating and Tasks marks.
items.fix: "You mentioned you've just got engaged. Is part of the worry what this means for having a family?"

items.fail: Prescribing for hirsutism with no metabolic screen and no plan for the infrequent periods.
items.why: "Management plan not in line with current UK best practice." PCOS needs glucose status, lipids, BP and a withdrawal bleed at least every 3–4 months (RCOG GTG 33).
items.fix: Say the three parts aloud: symptoms, sugar and heart risk, and protecting the womb lining.

items.fail: Starting a combined pill without checking BMI category, BP or VTE risk, or choosing co-cyprindiol first line.
items.why: UKMEC 2025 sets the combined pill at UKMEC 2 for BMI 30–34 and UKMEC 3 at 35 or more; co-cyprindiol carries a higher VTE risk (MHRA, June 2013).
items.fix: "At your weight the pill is still suitable. I'll check your blood pressure before we start."

items.fail: "Just lose some weight and it'll improve," said as a throwaway line.
items.why: Examiners flag judgemental language. It reinforces her self-blame and she disengages.
items.fix: "The weight is harder for you because of PCOS. What's one change that feels doable?"

items.why: "Language not easily understood by the patient."
items.fix: "A bit more of the male-type hormone", "not releasing an egg every month", "the womb lining needs to shed regularly".

items.fail: Closing with "any questions?" and no mention of what happens when she wants to conceive.
items.why: Fails to connect the plan to her concern, and misses pre-conception care.
items.fix: "When you're ready for a baby, come back first: folic acid, a sugar check and a clear referral plan."

timeMap.d: She opens with a list and "I feel disgusting". Let her finish; that word is the door to the real consultation.
Cycle pattern and last period, hirsutism and acne timeline, mimic screen (galactorrhoea, Cushing's features), family history of diabetes.
Mood and body image, then the engagement and the fertility fear. Ask a direct safety question about mood.
Name PCOS kindly. Fertility reassurance. Metabolic tests. Combined pill for cycles and hair. One realistic lifestyle goal she chooses.
Mood safety-net, bleed at least every 3–4 months, pre-conception visit, review in about 3 months, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes something for the hair and gives a diet leaflet; never names PCOS or explains it; misses the fertility fear and "I feel disgusting"; no metabolic screening or endometrial protection; frames weight as willpower.

wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: surfaces the fertility fear gently and answers it with honest, specific reassurance; explicitly lifts the self-blame; screens mood with a safety question; checks UKMEC at her BMI; links a pre-conception plan to the engagement; teach-back that leaves her ready to talk to her fiancé.

avoid.instead: "The weight is harder for you because of the condition, not a lack of effort. Let's find one change that feels doable."
avoid.why: Blaming language confirms her shame and loses the Relating domain.

SCA_MODELS.text: No, nothing like that. Just fed up with myself.

Let me give this a name, because it helps. Your periods, the hair and skin, and your test results fit polycystic ovary syndrome, PCOS. It's very common, it's a hormone imbalance, and it is not something you've caused. The difficulty losing weight is partly the condition itself, not a lack of willpower.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names PCOS kindly and removes self-blame

SCA_MODELS.text: So it's not just me being lazy?

Not at all. And on children, here's the honest picture: PCOS is one of the most treatable causes of difficulty getting pregnant. Many women with it conceive naturally, weight loss often brings ovulation back, and if needed there are effective treatments to help you ovulate. You are not broken.
(tearful) I really needed to hear that.

It's more than the hair and weight, though. PCOS can raise the risk of diabetes over time, especially with your family history, so I'd like a blood sugar test and cholesterol, and I'll check your blood pressure. And because your periods are infrequent, the womb lining needs to shed at least every three to four months to keep it healthy.

For the periods, hair and skin, a combined pill is usually the first step. It regulates bleeds, protects the lining and reduces hair and acne over several months. It's still suitable at your weight. There are also creams and hair-removal options. How does that sound?
SCA_MODELS.why: First-line symptom treatment with realistic timeframe and UKMEC check

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay, but what about the weight? Is there a tablet?

Weight-loss injections are only for people who meet strict criteria, and I'll check honestly whether you do. What usually works best is a realistic plan and support rather than another crash diet. What would feel doable for you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Answers the request honestly and shares the decision

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe more walking. I could manage that.

That's a great start, and I'll refer you to local weight-management support too. When you and your fiancé are ready to try for a baby, come back first. We'll start folic acid, check your sugar, and plan early referral if you need help ovulating.
SCA_MODELS.why: Pre-conception pathway linked to her concern

SCA_MODELS.text: If your mood drops or you ever feel unsafe, please contact us straight away, and ring 111 or 999 in a crisis. Also get in touch if you go more than three months without a bleed before we've sorted the pill. I'd like to see you in about three months to review the pill, your results and how you're feeling.
Thank you. I came in feeling like my body was against me.
So, to recap: blood tests and a blood pressure check, starting the pill, more walking, weight support, and a plan for when you want a baby. What will you tell your fiancé tonight?
That it's PCOS, it's common, and we can still have a family. I think I'll actually tell him now.

SCA_STEM.name: Bethan Lloyd
pmh: Infrequent periods (every 2–3 months), unwanted facial and body hair, acne
SCA_STEM.recent: Blood tests and pelvic ultrasound arranged at a previous appointment; results filed and consistent with polycystic ovary syndrome. Not yet discussed with her.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation to discuss irregular periods, excess hair and difficulty losing weight.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: International evidence-based PCOS guideline 2023 (international) · RCOG Green-top Guideline 33 (2014) · NICE NG257 (2026) · NICE NG246 · UKMEC 2025 · MHRA Drug Safety Update (June 2013)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Two of three Rotterdam features, with mimics excluded, make the diagnosis. Name it kindly, then manage the whole condition: metabolic risk, endometrial protection, symptoms, fertility and mood.

points.t: Two of three: irregular or absent ovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (or raised AMH in adults), after excluding thyroid disease, raised prolactin and non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (international guideline 2023). A Lancet consensus (May 2026) renamed the condition PMOS; a UK guideline (GID-NG10436) is in development and not yet published.

Check glycaemic status at diagnosis and then every 1–3 years (international guideline 2023), plus lipids and blood pressure. A family history of type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 31 raise her risk. Even modest weight loss improves cycles, hyperandrogenism and ovulation; NICE NG246 covers weight-management support.

With infrequent periods, aim for a withdrawal bleed at least every 3–4 months (RCOG GTG 33), using a combined pill or a cyclical progestogen (dose and duration per BNF). The combined pill is UKMEC 2 at BMI 30–34 (UKMEC 2025), so it remains an option for her.

The combined pill is first line for hirsutism and irregular cycles (international guideline 2023), with cosmetic measures and topical eflornithine (stop if no benefit at 4 months, per SPC). Consider anti-androgens only after at least 6 months, and always with reliable contraception. Co-cyprindiol carries a higher VTE risk and is second line (MHRA Drug Safety Update, June 2013). Acne follows the usual acne pathway.

PCOS is a common, treatable cause of anovulation, and most women with it conceive. Weight loss can restore ovulation; letrozole is first-line ovulation induction under specialist care (international guideline 2023). NICE NG257 advises earlier referral when there is a known cause of infertility. Before conception: folic acid (400 micrograms; BMI alone does not need the higher dose — NICE NG247) and a glucose check.
Screen everyone with PCOS for depression and anxiety, and be alert to disordered eating (international guideline 2023). Her "I feel disgusting" is a clinical cue, not small talk.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question first; let her describe the symptoms and her reading on PCOS before sharing results.
Engagement, body image, previous diet attempts, support from her fiancé.
Picked up "I feel disgusting" and the engagement, and explored them rather than moving straight to prescribing.
Idea (body "against her", a tablet will fix it); hidden fertility fear and low mood; expectation of a quick fix.
Reviews filed bloods/ultrasound; HbA1c or glucose status, lipids, BP; confirms mimics excluded (TSH, prolactin, 17-OHP).
PCOS against thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, non-classic CAH and Cushing's; screens for depression.
Asks about rapid virilisation or features of Cushing's; checks mood and self-harm thoughts.
Names PCOS kindly by Rotterdam criteria; explains that weight difficulty is partly the condition.
Combined pill (UKMEC 2 at BMI 31) for cycles, endometrium and hirsutism; cosmetic and topical options; realistic timeframes; honest answer on weight medicines.
Metabolic risk with family history of T2DM; endometrial protection; mood and body image; pre-conception care.
Review at about 3 months; mood safety-net; come back before trying to conceive; bleed at least every 3–4 months.

social.t: Visible symptoms such as hirsutism and acne can lead to avoidance, low self-esteem and strain in relationships. Newly engaged, she may be carrying shame she has not shared with her partner.
Weight-related shame reduces engagement with care. Use neutral language, ask permission to discuss weight, and focus on health gains rather than numbers.

legal.t: Metformin and spironolactone for PCOS features are off-label. Explain this, record the discussion and her agreement, and follow the BNF (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Local commissioning often sets BMI and other criteria for NHS-funded fertility treatment. Explain early, so weight goals are linked to a clear purpose.

professional.t: No UK PCOS guideline is published yet (GID-NG10436 in development). NICE NG257 removed its PCOS-specific recommendations. Say which source you are using and label the international guideline as such.
Present the combined pill, cyclical progestogen and cosmetic options with their trade-offs, and let her choose (GMC decision-making and consent guidance 2020).

community.t: Verity (the UK PCOS charity) for peer support and information; NHS weight-management services; NHS Talking Therapies if her mood needs support.

redFlags: Rapid-onset or severe virilisation (deepening voice, clitoromegaly): possible androgen-secreting tumour, needs urgent assessment
Features of Cushing's syndrome or galactorrhoea: exclude mimics before labelling PCOS
Low mood with hopelessness or self-harm thoughts
psychosocial: Recently engaged: the fertility question is urgent to her even if she has not said it
Previous diet attempts and the self-blame that followed
ice: Idea: "My body's against me; a tablet will fix the weight and the hair."
Concern: "I'm broken and won't be able to have children," plus low mood about her body
Expectation: a quick fix for weight and hair

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Name it clearly: "Your periods, the hair and skin changes and your test results fit polycystic ovary syndrome. It's common, it's hormonal, and it's manageable."
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: "Your hormones are slightly out of balance, so your ovaries don't release an egg every month. That's why periods are irregular, and why a bit more of the 'male-type' hormone causes hair and spots. It also makes your body handle sugar less efficiently, which is why weight is harder to shift. None of that is your fault."

management.reflectIce: "You told me you're frightened you can't have children. Let's deal with that honestly, because the news is much better than you fear."
management.psychosocial: Treat the mood and body image as part of the condition: validate, screen properly, and offer support. Agree one lifestyle goal she chooses rather than a lecture.
sharedPlan: Glucose status (HbA1c), lipids and BP now, then glycaemic review every 1–3 years
Combined pill for cycles, endometrial protection and hirsutism (UKMEC 2 at BMI 31); cosmetic and topical options; review at 3–6 months
Weight-management support; honest check of eligibility for weight medicines
Pre-conception visit: higher-dose folic acid (per BNF), glucose check, early referral if not ovulating
safetyNet: Contact the practice if mood worsens; 111 or 999 in a crisis
No bleed for more than 3 months before treatment is settled: get in touch

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed when it is treated as a cosmetic prescription. The request for "a tablet for weight and hair" is the entry point; the marks sit in naming PCOS kindly, the metabolic and endometrial tasks, and the fertility fear.

items.fail: Moving past "I feel disgusting" to ask about hair distribution and cycle length.
items.why: "Does not identify or respond to the patient's cues." That phrase is the emotional centre of the consultation.
items.fix: Reflect it back: "That's a strong word to use about yourself. How have you been in yourself?" Then follow where it leads.

items.fail: Never asking about the engagement, so the fertility fear stays hidden and she leaves still believing she is "broken".
items.why: The hidden agenda is the real consultation. Missing it caps both Relating and Tasks marks.
items.fix: "You mentioned you've just got engaged. Is part of the worry what this means for having a family?"

items.fail: Prescribing for hirsutism with no metabolic screen and no plan for the infrequent periods.
items.why: "Management plan not in line with current UK best practice." PCOS needs glucose status, lipids, BP and a withdrawal bleed at least every 3–4 months (RCOG GTG 33).
items.fix: Say the three parts aloud: symptoms, sugar and heart risk, and protecting the womb lining.

items.fail: Starting a combined pill without checking BMI category, BP or VTE risk, or choosing co-cyprindiol first line.
items.why: UKMEC 2025 sets the combined pill at UKMEC 2 for BMI 30–34 and UKMEC 3 at 35 or more; co-cyprindiol carries a higher VTE risk (MHRA, June 2013).
items.fix: "At your weight the pill is still suitable. I'll check your blood pressure before we start."

items.fail: "Just lose some weight and it'll improve," said as a throwaway line.
items.why: Examiners flag judgemental language. It reinforces her self-blame and she disengages.
items.fix: "The weight is harder for you because of PCOS. What's one change that feels doable?"

items.why: "Language not easily understood by the patient."
items.fix: "A bit more of the male-type hormone", "not releasing an egg every month", "the womb lining needs to shed regularly".

items.fail: Closing with "any questions?" and no mention of what happens when she wants to conceive.
items.why: Fails to connect the plan to her concern, and misses pre-conception care.
items.fix: "When you're ready for a baby, come back first: folic acid, a sugar check and a clear referral plan."
